## Introduction and overview {#intro}

  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
  Module               Theoretical Foundations of Deep Learning
  Official title       Fondements Théoriques du deep learning
  Instructors          S. GERCHINOVITZ, F. MALGOUYRES, E. PAUWELS, G. FRANCHI, N. THOME (master-mva.com, 2026–2027)
  Period               Semester 1 · period 1 (28/09/2026 – 08/01/2027)
  Credits and volume   5 ECTS · 30 h (lectures 25 h, labs 5 h) per the Université Paris-Saclay programme table
  Label                [Learning]{.badge .label} · domains on master-mva.com: Deep Learning, Theory
  Language             French, without distance teaching (Université Paris-Saclay course detail, “Langue d'enseignement”); not displayed on master-mva.com
  Assessment           master-mva.com (“Mode de validation”): labs (TP) 30 %, exam 70 %. Université Paris-Saclay course detail: one final exam (90 % of the grade) and one take-home assignment with an algorithm implementation (10 % of the grade); for the resit, an exam whose grade replaces the previous grades; nature of the assessment “Evaluation Continue non Intégrale”. The two official sources give different weights.
  Prerequisites        Basic notions of analysis, statistics and machine learning, and Python programming (both sources); the Université Paris-Saclay detail adds a Master 1 in mathematics and the basics of optimisation and statistical learning
  -------------------- ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Audience**: a student with a good M1 in mathematics, computer science or physics who has already trained a network in PyTorch and wants to know which of its behaviours are theorems, which are open problems and which are folklore.

**Empirical first**: the same two-layer network reaches 100 % training accuracy on the scikit-learn digits whether the labels are the true ones or a random permutation of them (ch. 9). Test accuracy is 97.8 % in the first case and 8.1 % in the second. Classical capacity bounds cannot tell the two runs apart; this course builds the tools to say what can.

The course is a mathematical reading of deep learning for classification and regression. It follows a network from its definition to its training, its approximation power, its generalisation and its reliability. Each step pairs a theorem with a small experiment. The optimisation chapters extend [Convex Optimization and Applications in Machine Learning](../s1-convex-optimization/index.html); the generalisation chapters extend [Introduction to Statistical Learning](../s1-intro-statistical-learning/index.html); the practice of networks is in [Deep Learning](../s1-deep-learning/index.html).

### What you will be able to do

-   Write a feed-forward or convolutional network as a composition of maps, and prove that a ReLU network is piecewise affine in its input and piecewise polynomial in its parameters.
-   Derive back-propagation, bound its cost, and explain exploding and vanishing gradients through products of Jacobians.
-   Describe the critical points of the training loss of linear and wide networks, and prove the implicit bias of gradient descent towards minimum-norm solutions.
-   State and use convergence results for gradient methods on non-convex functions: strict saddles, the Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz property, the Polyak–Łojasiewicz inequality.
-   Prove a universal approximation theorem, and quantify approximation with Barron's theorem, depth separation and Yarotsky's constructions.
-   Bound the generalisation error of a network with VC dimension and Rademacher complexity, and explain why such bounds are often vacuous.
-   Derive the risk of minimum-norm least squares and reproduce the double-descent curve.
-   Compute Bayesian posteriors, Laplace and variational approximations, and use MC dropout and ensembles to estimate predictive uncertainty.
-   Measure calibration, predict failures and detect out-of-distribution inputs, with the metrics used in safety-critical applications.
-   Bound the sensitivity of a network to perturbations and to individual training points.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026–2027)

The course description on master-mva.com states that the main objective is to present the mathematical formulation of deep neural networks used for classification and regression. It announces the problems raised by these models and representative results of current research on parameter optimisation, the properties of networks, their expressivity, their complexity, and phenomena that are still unexplained, such as double descent and implicit regularisation.

It then links these results to the practice of the algorithms, with a view to robustness (uncertainty, stability). Practical sessions (TP) help students understand some properties of deep networks intuitively, implement learning algorithms on concrete problems and place the mathematical properties in their applied context.

The teaching team listed on master-mva.com is Sébastien Gerchinovitz (researcher, IRT Saint-Exupéry), François Malgouyres (professor, Institut de Mathématiques de Toulouse), Édouard Pauwels (maître de conférences, IRIT), Nicolas Thome (professor, Sorbonne Université, ISIR) and Gianni Franchi (teacher-researcher in trustworthy AI, ENSTA Paris). The Université Paris-Saclay detail states the objective as presenting representative research results on the mathematical justification of deep learning algorithms, then linking them to practice.

The table matches every official item — the “Thèmes abordés” of master-mva.com, each bullet of its ten announced sessions, and each item of the Université Paris-Saclay “Programme / plan / contenus” — with the section of these notes that teaches it.

### Where this course fits in the programme

Official prerequisites: basic notions of analysis, statistics, machine learning and Python programming; the Université Paris-Saclay detail adds a Master 1 in mathematics with the basics of optimisation and statistical learning.

-   **Preparation** — the refreshers [Probability and Statistics](../s0-refresher-probability-statistics/index.html) (concentration, Gaussian computations), [Linear Algebra, Analysis and Optimization](../s0-refresher-linear-algebra-optimization/index.html) (SVD, gradients, descent methods) and [Scientific Python, NumPy and PyTorch](../s0-refresher-python-scientific-computing/index.html) (autograd, the labs).
-   **Related courses of the same semester** — [Deep Learning](../s1-deep-learning/index.html) (architectures and training practice), [Convex Optimization and Applications in Machine Learning](../s1-convex-optimization/index.html), [Introduction to Statistical Learning](../s1-intro-statistical-learning/index.html) (risk bounds), [Probabilistic Graphical Models and Deep Generative Models](../s1-probabilistic-graphical-models/index.html) (variational inference), [Computational Statistics](../s1-computational-statistics/index.html), [Optimal Transport for Machine Learning](../s1-optimal-transport-ml/index.html) (Wasserstein GANs) and [Turing Seminar: An Introduction to AGI Safety](../s1-turing-seminar-ai-safety/index.html) (robustness).
-   **Semester 2 courses that build on it** — [Bayesian Machine Learning](../s2-bayesian-ml/index.html), [Kernel Methods for Machine Learning](../s2-kernel-methods/index.html) (neural tangent kernel), [Large Random Matrices and Applications to Machine Learning](../s2-random-matrices-ml/index.html) (double descent), [Deep Learning in Practice / Advanced Deep Learning](../s2-deep-learning-in-practice/index.html), [Responsible Machine Learning](../s2-responsible-ml/index.html), [Multimodal Explainable AI (XAI)](../s2-multimodal-xai/index.html), [Generative Models for Images](../s2-generative-models-images/index.html) and [Learning Physical Phenomena: Metamodelling and Uncertainty Quantification](../s2-physics-learning-uq/index.html).

### Course outline

-   **Review: calculus, probability and optimisation from M1** — the chain rule, the descent lemma, concentration inequalities, Gaussian conditioning and the pseudo-inverse.
-   **The learning problem and neural network models** — risk, Bayes predictor, risk estimation, the three errors, feed-forward and convolutional networks, the zoo, GANs, piecewise-affine predictions.
-   **The prediction as a function of the parameters; back-propagation** — piecewise polynomials in θ, symmetries, non-convexity, non-coercivity, back-propagation, exploding and vanishing gradients.
-   **Landscape of the objective function** — critical points, linear networks, implicit regularisation, stability of factorisations, wide networks.
-   **Non-convex optimisation** — gradient descent on smooth functions, strict saddles, the Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz property, global convergence for over-parameterised least squares, stochastic gradient.
-   **Robust deep learning I** — Lipschitz stability, stability to deformations, influence functions, typology of uncertainty, Bayesian linear regression (lab).
-   **Robust deep learning II** — Laplace approximation, variational Bayes by Backprop, dropout as regularisation and as variational inference (lab).
-   **Robust deep learning III** — metrics for regression, ensembles, evidential models, calibration, failure prediction, out-of-distribution detection (lab).
-   **Expressivity** — universal approximation, Barron's theorem, depth separation, super-approximation.
-   **Generalisation error** — finite classes, Rademacher complexity, VC dimension, bounds for networks.
-   **Open questions; double descent** — the generalisation puzzle, guarantees from a validation set, the exact risk of minimum-norm least squares.
-   **Research directions and open problems** — implicit bias in classification, kernel and mean-field limits, benign overfitting, edge of stability, non-smooth automatic differentiation, non-vacuous bounds, conformal prediction, certified robustness, theory of GANs (self-study).

### How to study this module

-   Read ch. 0 before the first session, and redo its proofs: the descent lemma, Hoeffding's inequality and the pseudo-inverse are used without warning later.
-   After each session, do the exercises of the *Practice* column, then rerun the chapter's code and change one parameter at a time.
-   Every code block runs on a laptop CPU in a few seconds with NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn and PyTorch; no data are downloaded.
-   For the three labs (sessions 5–7), start from the code blocks of ch. 5, 6 and 7, which are minimal versions of the official lab subjects.
-   Keep a list of the assumptions of each theorem: most of the open problems of ch. 10–11 are exactly the gaps between those assumptions and practice.

## 0. Review: calculus, probability and optimisation from M1 {#ch0}

The proofs of this course use five M1 tools again and again. This chapter states them once, with the short proofs, so that later chapters can cite them by number.

::: def
[Definition 0.1 — Jacobian and chain rule]{.tag} For a differentiable map $F : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^m$, the Jacobian $J_F(x) \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ collects the partial derivatives $\partial F_i / \partial x_j$. For a composition,
$$
J_{G \circ F}(x) = J_G(F(x))\, J_F(x).
$$

For a scalar function $\ell : \mathbb{R}^m \to \mathbb{R}$, the gradient of $\ell \circ F$ is obtained by applying the *transposed* Jacobian to the gradient of $\ell$:
$$
\nabla (\ell \circ F)(x) = J_F(x)^\top\, \nabla \ell(F(x)).
$$

Back-propagation (ch. 2) is this identity applied layer after layer, from the output back to the input.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.2 — Descent lemma]{.tag} Let $f : \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable with an $L$-Lipschitz gradient. For all $x, y$:
$$
f(y) \le f(x) + \langle \nabla f(x), y - x \rangle + \frac{L}{2} \|y - x\|^2 .
$$

In particular, one gradient step $x^+ = x - \nabla f(x)/L$ decreases $f$ by at least $\|\nabla f(x)\|^2 / (2L)$.

::: proof
Write $f(y) - f(x) - \langle \nabla f(x), y - x\rangle$ as the integral over $t \in [0, 1]$ of $\langle \nabla f(x + t(y - x)) - \nabla f(x), y - x \rangle$.

By Cauchy–Schwarz and the Lipschitz property, the integrand is at most $L t \|y - x\|^2$, whose integral is $L\|y - x\|^2/2$.

For the second claim, put $y = x^+$: the right-hand side becomes $f(x) - \|\nabla f(x)\|^2/L + \|\nabla f(x)\|^2/(2L)$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: thm
[Theorem 0.3 — Hoeffding and McDiarmid inequalities]{.tag} Let $Z_1, \dots, Z_n$ be independent random variables.

-   **Hoeffding.** If $Z_i \in [a_i, b_i]$ almost surely, then for every $t > 0$
    $$
    \mathbb{P}\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n (Z_i - \mathbb{E} Z_i) \ge t\Big) \le \exp\Big(-\frac{2t^2}{\sum_i (b_i - a_i)^2}\Big).
    $$
-   **McDiarmid.** If changing the $i$-th argument of $g$ changes its value by at most $c_i$, then
    $$
    \mathbb{P}\big(g(Z_1, \dots, Z_n) - \mathbb{E}\, g \ge t\big) \le \exp\Big(-\frac{2t^2}{\sum_i c_i^2}\Big).
    $$

*Key step of the proof*: Hoeffding's lemma bounds the moment generating function of a centred variable in $[a, b]$ by $e^{\lambda^2 (b - a)^2 / 8}$; Markov's inequality applied to $e^{\lambda S}$ and an optimisation in $\lambda$ conclude. McDiarmid applies the same lemma to the martingale differences of $g$ (Boucheron, Lugosi and Massart, 2013, ch. 2 and 6).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.4 — Gaussian conditioning]{.tag} Let $w \sim \mathcal{N}(m_0, S_0)$ and, given $w$, let $y \sim \mathcal{N}(\Phi w, \beta^{-1} I)$. Then the conditional law of $w$ given $y$ is Gaussian, $\mathcal{N}(m, S)$, with
$$
S^{-1} = S_0^{-1} + \beta\, \Phi^\top \Phi, \qquad m = S\,\big(S_0^{-1} m_0 + \beta\, \Phi^\top y\big).
$$

::: proof
Up to terms that do not depend on $w$, the log-density of $w$ given $y$ is
$$
-\tfrac12 (w - m_0)^\top S_0^{-1} (w - m_0) - \tfrac{\beta}{2} \|y - \Phi w\|^2 .
$$

Its quadratic part in $w$ is $-\tfrac12 w^\top S^{-1} w$ and its linear part is $w^\top (S_0^{-1} m_0 + \beta \Phi^\top y)$.

Completing the square identifies a Gaussian with precision $S^{-1}$ and mean $m$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.5 — Pseudo-inverse and minimum-norm solutions]{.tag} Let $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$ have the singular value decomposition $X = U \Sigma V^\top$. Its pseudo-inverse is $X^+ = V \Sigma^+ U^\top$, where $\Sigma^+$ inverts the non-zero singular values.

If the system $Xw = y$ has a solution, then $w^+ = X^+ y$ is its unique solution of minimal Euclidean norm, and the unique solution lying in the row space $\mathrm{Im}(X^\top)$.

::: proof
Every solution writes $w^+ + v$ with $v \in \ker X$. The vector $w^+$ lies in $\mathrm{Im}(V\Sigma^+) \subset \mathrm{Im}(X^\top)$, which is orthogonal to $\ker X$.

By Pythagoras, $\|w^+ + v\|^2 = \|w^+\|^2 + \|v\|^2$, minimal exactly when $v = 0$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 0

-   Gradients of compositions are transposed Jacobians applied to a gradient: back-propagation.
-   With an $L$-Lipschitz gradient, a step $1/L$ decreases $f$ by at least $\|\nabla f\|^2 / (2L)$.
-   Bounded independent sums concentrate at rate $1/\sqrt{n}$; Gaussian prior and likelihood give a Gaussian posterior.
-   The pseudo-inverse picks the minimum-norm solution, which lies in the row space.
:::

## 1. The learning problem and neural network models {#ch1}

This chapter fixes the objects of the course: the risk a network must minimise, how to estimate it, and what a network computes.

### 1.1 Classification and regression

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Risk, empirical risk, Bayes risk]{.tag} Data are pairs $(X, Y)$ drawn from an unknown distribution $P$ on $\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$. A **loss** $\ell(\hat y, y) \ge 0$ measures the cost of predicting $\hat y$ when the truth is $y$.

The **risk** of a predictor $f$ and its empirical counterpart on a sample $(x_i, y_i)_{i \le n}$ are
$$
R(f) = \mathbb{E}\big[\ell(f(X), Y)\big], \qquad \widehat R_n(f) = \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n \ell(f(x_i), y_i).
$$

The **Bayes risk** $R^\ast$ is the infimum of $R$ over all measurable predictors.

-   **Regression**: $\mathcal{Y} = \mathbb{R}$ and the square loss $\ell(\hat y, y) = (\hat y - y)^2$.
-   **Classification** with $K$ classes: the 0–1 loss $\mathbb{1}[\hat y \ne y]$ for evaluation, and the cross-entropy $-\log p_y$ of a vector of class probabilities $p$ for training.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.2 — Bayes predictors]{.tag} For the square loss, the Bayes predictor is the regression function $f^\ast(x) = \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = x]$, and for every $f$
$$
R(f) - R(f^\ast) = \mathbb{E}\big[(f(X) - f^\ast(X))^2\big].
$$

For the 0–1 loss, the Bayes classifier predicts $\arg\max_k \mathbb{P}(Y = k \mid X = x)$.

::: proof
Expand the square around $f^\ast(X)$:
$$
(f(X) - Y)^2 = (f(X) - f^\ast(X))^2 + 2 (f(X) - f^\ast(X))(f^\ast(X) - Y) + (f^\ast(X) - Y)^2 .
$$

Conditionally on $X$, the cross term has zero mean because $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X] = f^\ast(X)$; taking expectations gives the identity, whose right-hand side is non-negative.

For the 0–1 loss, the conditional risk of predicting $k$ at $x$ is $1 - \mathbb{P}(Y = k \mid X = x)$, minimal at the most probable class. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 1.2 Risk estimation

The risk is never observed. The cleanest estimate uses data that played no role in training.

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.3 — Risk estimation on a test set]{.tag} Let $f$ be fixed independently of a test sample of size $m$, and let the loss take values in $[0, 1]$. With probability at least $1 - \delta$,
$$
\big|\widehat R_{\mathrm{test}}(f) - R(f)\big| \le \sqrt{\frac{\log(2/\delta)}{2m}} .
$$

::: proof
The $m$ test losses are independent, in $[0, 1]$, with mean $R(f)$. Apply Hoeffding's inequality (Theorem 0.3) to the sum and to its opposite with $t = m\varepsilon$, and take a union bound over the two sides. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 1.4 — How precise is a test accuracy?]{.tag} With $m = 10\,000$ test images and $\delta = 0.05$, the half-width is $\sqrt{\log(40)/20\,000}$, that is
$$
\varepsilon \approx 0.0136 .
$$

A gain of 0.5 % between two models is not certified by this bound. Choosing among $k$ models on the same test set replaces $\log(2/\delta)$ by $\log(2k/\delta)$.
:::

### 1.3 Approximation, estimation and optimisation errors

A trained network is limited by its architecture, its finite sample and its training algorithm. Each limitation has a cost.

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.5 — Decomposition of the excess risk]{.tag} Let $\mathcal{F}$ be the class of functions realised by an architecture, $f_{\mathcal F}$ a minimiser of the risk over $\mathcal{F}$, $\hat f_n$ a minimiser of the empirical risk over $\mathcal{F}$, and $\tilde f$ the output of the training algorithm. Then
$$
R(\tilde f) - R^\ast = \underbrace{R(f_{\mathcal F}) - R^\ast}_{\text{approximation}} + \underbrace{R(\hat f_n) - R(f_{\mathcal F})}_{\text{estimation}} + \underbrace{R(\tilde f) - R(\hat f_n)}_{\text{optimisation}} .
$$

Moreover, the estimation error is at most $2 \sup_{f \in \mathcal F} |R(f) - \widehat R_n(f)|$.

::: proof
The identity is a telescoping sum. For the bound, write $R(\hat f_n) - R(f_{\mathcal F})$ as the sum of three differences: $R(\hat f_n) - \widehat R_n(\hat f_n)$, then $\widehat R_n(\hat f_n) - \widehat R_n(f_{\mathcal F})$, then $\widehat R_n(f_{\mathcal F}) - R(f_{\mathcal F})$.

The middle difference is non-positive because $\hat f_n$ minimises $\widehat R_n$; each of the two others is at most the supremum. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Approximation is studied in [ch. 8](#ch8), estimation in [ch. 9](#ch9), optimisation in [ch. 3](#ch3) and [ch. 4](#ch4). Classically, enlarging $\mathcal{F}$ lowers the first term and raises the second: the test error is U-shaped in the model size.

::: note
[The modern regime: implicit regularisation and double descent]{.tag} Deep networks are trained far past interpolation of the training set, and their test error often keeps *decreasing*. Belkin, Hsu, Ma and Mandal (2019) called the curve *double descent*: a U-shape, a peak at the interpolation threshold, then a second descent.

Explaining it needs two ingredients: which interpolant the algorithm selects (implicit regularisation, Proposition 3.4), and the risk of that interpolant (Theorem 10.2).
:::

### 1.4 Feed-forward and convolutional networks

::: def
[Definition 1.6 — Feed-forward network]{.tag} Fix widths $n_0 = d, n_1, \dots, n_L$ and an activation $\sigma : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ applied entrywise, typically the ReLU $\sigma(t) = \max(t, 0)$. The parameters are $\theta = (W_\ell, b_\ell)_{\ell \le L}$ with $W_\ell \in \mathbb{R}^{n_\ell \times n_{\ell - 1}}$. The network computes $a_0 = x$ and
$$
z_\ell = W_\ell\, a_{\ell - 1} + b_\ell, \qquad a_\ell = \sigma(z_\ell) \quad (\ell < L), \qquad f_\theta(x) = z_L .
$$

The **depth** is $L$, the **width** is $\max_\ell n_\ell$, and the number of parameters is $W = \sum_\ell n_\ell (n_{\ell - 1} + 1)$. For classification, $f_\theta(x) \in \mathbb{R}^K$ is a vector of logits, turned into probabilities by the softmax.
:::

:::: def
[Definition 1.7 — Convolutional layer]{.tag} For a signal $x \in \mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{Z}}$ (or an image on $\mathbb{Z}^2$) and a filter $w$ supported on $\{-k, \dots, k\}$, the convolutional layer computes
$$
(w \ast x)(u) = \sum_{|v| \le k} w(v)\, x(u - v),
$$
followed by a bias, an activation and often a subsampling (stride or pooling). With $C$ input channels and $C'$ output channels, the layer is a sum of such convolutions, with $C C' (2k + 1)$ weights whatever the size of the signal: the weights are *shared* across positions.

::: prop
[Proposition 1.8 — Translation equivariance]{.tag} Let $(T_s x)(u) = x(u - s)$. A convolution commutes with translations:
$$
w \ast (T_s x) = T_s (w \ast x).
$$

So does every entrywise activation; without subsampling, a stack of such layers is translation-equivariant, and a final global average makes it invariant.

*Proof*: $\sum_v w(v)\, x(u - v - s)$ is the value of $w \ast x$ at $u - s$.
:::
::::

### 1.5 A tour of the zoo

The theorems below concern feed-forward networks; the same questions arise for the architectures used in practice.

-   **Recurrent networks** apply the same cell along a sequence, $h_t = \sigma(W h_{t-1} + U x_t + b)$. Back-propagation through time multiplies $T$ Jacobians of one cell, so gradients explode or vanish ([ch. 2](#ch2)); the LSTM of Hochreiter and Schmidhuber (1997) adds a gated additive memory.
-   **Transformers** (Vaswani et al., 2017) replace recurrence by attention: for queries $Q$, keys $K$ and values $V$, a head computes $\mathrm{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})\, V$, stacked with residual connections, normalisations and feed-forward blocks.
-   **Representation learning** reuses an intermediate layer $a_\ell(x)$ for other tasks: auto-encoders, self-supervised and contrastive learning.
-   **Generative adversarial networks** (GANs; Goodfellow et al., 2014) train a generator $G$, mapping noise to samples, against a discriminator $D$ that separates them from data. **FairGAN** (Xu, Yuan, Zhang and Wu, 2018) adds a discriminator that tries to recover a protected attribute, so that the generated data carry less information about it.

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.9 — Optimal discriminator of a GAN (Goodfellow et al., 2014)]{.tag} Let $p$ be the data density and $q$ the density of $G(z)$, and consider
$$
V(D, G) = \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p}[\log D(x)] + \mathbb{E}_{x \sim q}[\log(1 - D(x))].
$$

For fixed $G$, the maximiser over all functions $D$ with values in $(0, 1)$ is $D^\ast = p / (p + q)$, and
$$
\max_D V(D, G) = 2\, \mathrm{JS}(p, q) - \log 4,
$$
where $\mathrm{JS}$ is the Jensen–Shannon divergence. The generator therefore minimises a divergence, uniquely at $q = p$.

::: proof
The value is the integral of $p(x) \log D(x) + q(x) \log(1 - D(x))$. For fixed $a, b > 0$, the function $t \mapsto a \log t + b \log(1 - t)$ is maximal at $t = a/(a + b)$, so the maximiser is pointwise.

Substituting $D^\ast$ gives $\mathrm{KL}(p \,\|\, m) + \mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, m) - \log 4$ with $m = (p + q)/2$, which is $2\,\mathrm{JS}(p, q) - \log 4$.

The JS divergence is non-negative and vanishes only when $p = q$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For disjoint supports, $\mathrm{JS}(p, q) = \log 2$ whatever their distance, and the generator gets no gradient: hence the Wasserstein GAN (Arjovsky, Chintala and Bottou, 2017; see [Optimal Transport for Machine Learning](../s1-optimal-transport-ml/index.html)).

### 1.6 A piecewise-affine prediction as a function of the input

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.10 — ReLU networks are piecewise affine]{.tag} Let $f_\theta$ be a ReLU network (Definition 1.6). For every input $x$, call **activation pattern** the vector of signs $\mathbb{1}[z_\ell(x) > 0]$ of all hidden units. On the set of inputs sharing a given pattern, $f_\theta$ coincides with an affine map. Hence $f_\theta$ is continuous and piecewise affine, with at most one affine piece per realised pattern.

::: proof
Let $D_\ell(x)$ be the diagonal matrix of the pattern of layer $\ell$, so that $a_\ell = D_\ell(x) z_\ell$.

On a set where all the matrices $D_\ell$ are constant, an induction on the layers shows that $z_\ell$ is affine in $x$.

Indeed $z_1$ is affine, and if $z_\ell$ is affine then so is $z_{\ell + 1} = W_{\ell+1} D_\ell z_\ell + b_{\ell + 1}$.

Continuity holds because ReLU is continuous. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.11 — One hidden layer on the line]{.tag} A ReLU network with one hidden layer of $m$ units and a scalar input is piecewise affine with at most $m + 1$ pieces. Conversely, every continuous piecewise-affine function on $\mathbb{R}$ with $m + 1$ pieces is realised by such a network with $m$ hidden units, plus an affine term.

::: proof
Each unit $\sigma(w_j x + b_j)$ with $w_j \neq 0$ has one kink, at $x = -b_j/w_j$; a sum of such functions can only change slope at these $m$ points.

Conversely, if $g$ has kinks at $t_1 < \dots < t_m$ with slope jumps $c_j$, then $g(x) - \sum_j c_j \sigma(x - t_j)$ has no kink, so it is affine. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Depth can multiply the number of pieces ([ch. 8](#ch8)), but random networks use little of this capacity.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

def random_layers(widths):
    """He-initialised weights and small biases for a ReLU network."""
    return [(rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(2 / m), (m, k)), rng.normal(0, 0.5, k))
            for m, k in zip(widths[:-1], widths[1:])]

def activation_patterns(x, layers):
    """Sign pattern of every hidden unit, for each input point of a 1-D grid."""
    h, pats = x[:, None], []
    for W, b in layers[:-1]:
        z = h @ W + b
        pats.append(z > 0)
        h = np.maximum(z, 0.0)
    return np.hstack(pats)

x = np.linspace(-4, 4, 40_001)
for widths in [(1, 16, 1), (1, 8, 8, 1), (1, 4, 4, 4, 4, 1)]:
    counts = []
    for trial in range(10):
        P = activation_patterns(x, random_layers(widths))
        changes = np.any(P[1:] != P[:-1], axis=1).sum()
        counts.append(changes + 1)          # affine pieces of x -> f(x)
    print(f"widths {widths}: {sum(widths[1:-1])} units, "
          f"mean pieces {np.mean(counts):.1f}, max {max(counts)}")
```

With 16 hidden units in each case, the mean number of pieces on $[-4, 4]$ is 16.1 for one layer, 15.9 for two and 13.6 for four: it grows with the number of units, not exponentially with depth, as Hanin and Rolnick (2019) prove in expectation at initialisation.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 1

-   A held-out test set estimates the risk to within $\sqrt{\log(2/\delta)/(2m)}$.
-   The excess risk splits into approximation, estimation and optimisation errors.
-   With an optimal discriminator, a GAN generator minimises a Jensen–Shannon divergence.
-   A ReLU network is continuous and piecewise affine in its input, one piece per activation pattern.
:::

## 2. The prediction as a function of the parameters; back-propagation {#ch2}

Training sees $f_\theta$ as a function of $\theta$. This chapter describes its regularity and symmetries, and computes its gradient.

### 2.1 A piecewise-polynomial prediction in θ

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.1 — Piecewise-polynomial dependence on the parameters]{.tag} Fix an input $x$ and a ReLU network of depth $L$. The map $\theta \mapsto f_\theta(x)$ is continuous and piecewise polynomial. On each set of parameters that share the same activation pattern at $x$, it is a polynomial of degree at most $L$, affine in each pair $(W_\ell, b_\ell)$ separately.

The sets of constant pattern are defined by polynomial inequalities in $\theta$: they are semi-algebraic, a fact used in [ch. 4](#ch4).

::: proof
With the pattern matrices $D_\ell$ fixed, unroll Definition 1.6:
$$
f_\theta(x) = W_L D_{L-1}\big(W_{L-1} D_{L-2}(\cdots D_1 (W_1 x + b_1) \cdots) + b_{L-1}\big) + b_L .
$$

Expanding the products, each monomial contains at most one entry of $(W_\ell, b_\ell)$ for each layer $\ell$, hence the degree bound and the multi-affine structure.

The pattern is constant where the signs of the $z_\ell(x)$ are fixed, and each $z_\ell(x)$ is itself a polynomial in $\theta$ on such a set. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

For the square loss, the empirical risk is therefore piecewise polynomial of degree at most $2L$ in $\theta$: a smooth function on each piece, with kinks on the boundaries.

### 2.2 Basic properties of the cost function

::: def
[Definition 2.2 — Training objective]{.tag} Given data $(x_i, y_i)_{i \le n}$ and a loss $\ell$, the training objective is the empirical risk as a function of the parameters, possibly with weight decay $\lambda \ge 0$:
$$
F(\theta) = \frac1n \sum_{i=1}^n \ell\big(f_\theta(x_i), y_i\big) + \frac{\lambda}{2}\, \|\theta\|^2 .
$$
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.3 — Symmetries of ReLU networks]{.tag} The following transformations of $\theta$ leave the function $f_\theta$ unchanged, hence leave $F$ unchanged when $\lambda = 0$.

-   **Permutation.** Permute the units of a hidden layer $\ell$: the rows of $(W_\ell, b_\ell)$ and the columns of $W_{\ell + 1}$ by the same permutation.
-   **Rescaling.** For $c > 0$, replace $(W_\ell, b_\ell, W_{\ell + 1})$ by $(c W_\ell, c\, b_\ell, W_{\ell + 1}/c)$.

::: proof
A permutation of the units only reorders the terms of the sum computed by layer $\ell + 1$.

For the rescaling, ReLU is positively homogeneous, $\sigma(ct) = c\,\sigma(t)$ for $c > 0$; the factor $c$ multiplying $z_\ell$ goes through $\sigma$ and is cancelled by $W_{\ell + 1}/c$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 2.4 — The smallest deep network]{.tag} Take one scalar weight per layer, two layers, one data point $x = y = 1$ and no activation:
$$
F(a, b) = (ab - 1)^2 .
$$

-   The global minima form the hyperbola $ab = 1$: unbounded and not isolated, the rescaling orbit of Proposition 2.3.
-   The origin is a critical point. The Hessian there is the matrix with $0$ on the diagonal and $-2$ off it, with eigenvalues $\pm 2$: a strict saddle.
-   $F$ is not convex: $F(1, 1) = F(-1, -1) = 0$, but $F$ equals $1$ at their midpoint $(0, 0)$.
:::

:::: prop
[Corollary 2.5 — Non-convexity and non-coercivity]{.tag} Let $F$ be the objective of a ReLU network with $\lambda = 0$.

-   **Non-convexity.** Suppose that $F$ has a minimiser, that a hidden layer has two units, and that no minimiser of $F$ gives these two units identical incoming and outgoing weights. Then $F$ is not convex.
-   **Non-coercivity.** If some layer is not identically zero at a minimiser, $F$ has unbounded level sets and no isolated minimiser; it is not strongly convex near any minimiser.

With weight decay $\lambda > 0$, $F$ becomes coercive and has a minimiser, but the permutation symmetry, hence the non-convexity, remain.

::: proof
If $F$ were convex, its set of minimisers would be convex. Let $\theta^\ast$ be a minimiser and $\pi\theta^\ast$ its image under the swap of the two units; both are minimisers.

Their midpoint is then a minimiser, and it is invariant under the swap: the two units have identical weights, a contradiction.

For coercivity, the rescaling orbit of $\theta^\ast$ is an unbounded curve on which $F$ is constant. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

### 2.3 Back-propagation

::: thm
[Algorithm 2.6 — Back-propagation]{.tag} For one example $(x, y)$ and the network of Definition 1.6:

1.  **Forward pass.** Compute and store $z_\ell$ and $a_\ell$ for $\ell = 1, \dots, L$.
2.  **Output.** Set $\delta_L = \nabla_{z_L}\, \ell(z_L, y)$.
3.  **Backward pass.** For $\ell = L - 1, \dots, 1$, set
    $$
    \delta_\ell = \sigma'(z_\ell) \odot \big(W_{\ell + 1}^\top \delta_{\ell + 1}\big).
    $$
4.  **Gradients.** For every layer,
    $$
    \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial W_\ell} = \delta_\ell\, a_{\ell - 1}^\top, \qquad \frac{\partial \ell}{\partial b_\ell} = \delta_\ell .
    $$

For a mini-batch, the gradients of the examples are averaged.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.7 — Correctness and cost of back-propagation]{.tag} At every point where $\sigma$ is differentiable at all the $z_\ell$, the vector $\delta_\ell$ equals $\partial \ell / \partial z_\ell$, and the formulas of step 4 give the gradient. The backward pass costs at most twice the multiplications of the forward pass, whatever the number $W$ of parameters.

By contrast, finite differences need $W + 1$ forward passes.

::: proof
Induction from $\ell = L$ down. The map $z_\ell \mapsto z_{\ell+1}$, given by $z_{\ell+1} = W_{\ell+1}\sigma(z_\ell) + b_{\ell+1}$, has Jacobian $W_{\ell+1}\,\mathrm{diag}(\sigma'(z_\ell))$.

By the chain rule (Definition 0.1), $\partial \ell / \partial z_\ell$ is the transpose of this Jacobian applied to $\delta_{\ell + 1}$, which is step 3.

Since $z_\ell = W_\ell a_{\ell-1} + b_\ell$ depends on $W_\ell$ linearly, the derivative with respect to the entry $(i, j)$ of $W_\ell$ is $\delta_{\ell, i}\, a_{\ell - 1, j}$.

For the cost, layer $\ell$ costs $n_\ell n_{\ell - 1}$ multiplications forward; backward it needs one product by $W_\ell^\top$ and one outer product, each of the same size. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Back-propagation is reverse-mode automatic differentiation; its price is the memory needed to store every $z_\ell$. At a ReLU kink, PyTorch sets $\sigma'(0) = 0$, and the output need not be a gradient ([ch. 11](#ch11)).

```python
import numpy as np
import torch

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
d, m, n = 3, 5, 4
X = rng.normal(size=(n, d)); y = rng.normal(size=n)
W1, W2, w3 = rng.normal(size=(m, d)), rng.normal(size=(m, m)), rng.normal(size=m)

z1 = X @ W1.T; a1 = np.maximum(z1, 0)          # forward pass, storing z_l and a_l
z2 = a1 @ W2.T; a2 = np.maximum(z2, 0)
f = a2 @ w3

g_f = (f - y) / n                               # backward pass, loss = mean of (f - y)^2 / 2
g_w3 = a2.T @ g_f
d2 = np.outer(g_f, w3) * (z2 > 0)               # delta_2 = sigma'(z_2) * (w3 delta_3)
g_W2 = d2.T @ a1
d1 = (d2 @ W2) * (z1 > 0)                       # delta_1 = sigma'(z_1) * (W2^T delta_2)
g_W1 = d1.T @ X

T = lambda A: torch.tensor(A, requires_grad=True)
tW1, tW2, tw3 = T(W1), T(W2), T(w3)
tf = torch.relu(torch.relu(torch.tensor(X) @ tW1.T) @ tW2.T) @ tw3
(0.5 * ((tf - torch.tensor(y)) ** 2).mean()).backward()
err = max(np.abs(g - t.grad.numpy()).max() for g, t in [(g_W1, tW1), (g_W2, tW2), (g_w3, tw3)])
print(f"max |hand-made gradient - autograd| = {err:.1e}")
```

The hand-made gradient agrees with PyTorch's autograd to machine precision ($2.2 \times 10^{-16}$).

### 2.4 Exploding and vanishing gradients

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.8 — Gradients are products of matrices]{.tag} With $D_\ell = \mathrm{diag}(\sigma'(z_\ell))$, the Jacobian of a network with respect to its input is
$$
J_{f_\theta}(x) = W_L D_{L-1} W_{L-1} \cdots D_1 W_1 .
$$

For ReLU, $\|D_\ell\|_2 \le 1$, so $\|J_{f_\theta}(x)\|_2 \le \prod_\ell \|W_\ell\|_2$. Likewise, $\delta_\ell$ is a product of $L - \ell$ such factors applied to $\delta_L$.

::: proof
Apply the chain rule of Definition 0.1 to the composition of the maps $a_{\ell-1} \mapsto a_\ell$, whose Jacobians are $D_\ell W_\ell$, and use the sub-multiplicativity of the operator norm. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

A product of $L$ random matrices typically grows or decays geometrically in $L$. The initialisation decides which.

:::: prop
[Proposition 2.9 — Variance propagation and He initialisation]{.tag} Let the weights of layer $\ell + 1$ be independent $\mathcal{N}(0, s^2/n_\ell)$, the biases zero, and $\sigma$ the ReLU. Let $q_\ell$ be the second moment of one coordinate of $z_\ell$. Then

::: key
[Key result — variance propagation through ReLU layers]{.tag}
$$
q_{\ell + 1} = \frac{s^2}{2}\, q_\ell .
$$
:::

With $s^2 = 2$ (He et al., 2015) the second moment is preserved across layers. With $s^2 = 2g^2$ it is multiplied by $g^{2L}$ over $L$ layers. The back-propagated $\delta_\ell$ obey the same law under the usual approximation that treats the backward weights as independent of the forward activations.

::: proof
Coordinate $i$ of $z_{\ell+1}$ is $\sum_j W_{ij} a_{\ell, j}$ with $W$ independent of $a_\ell$, so its second moment is $(s^2/n_\ell)\, \mathbb{E}\|a_\ell\|^2$.

Given the previous layer, $z_\ell$ is a centred Gaussian vector, hence symmetric, so
$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\sigma(z_{\ell, j})^2\big] = \tfrac12\, \mathbb{E}\big[z_{\ell, j}^2\big].
$$

Summing over the $n_\ell$ units gives $\mathbb{E}\|a_\ell\|^2 = n_\ell q_\ell / 2$. The backward pass is the same computation with $W^\top$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
width, L = 200, 50
for gain in [0.8, 1.0, 1.2]:
    x = rng.normal(size=width)
    Ws, h = [], x
    for _ in range(L):                                    # forward pass, He scale times gain
        W = rng.normal(0, gain * np.sqrt(2 / width), (width, width))
        Ws.append((W, W @ h > 0)); h = np.maximum(W @ h, 0)
    g = rng.normal(size=width); g /= np.linalg.norm(g)    # backward: g <- W^T (mask * g)
    for W, mask in reversed(Ws):
        g = W.T @ (mask * g)
    print(f"gain {gain}: ||grad wrt input|| after {L} layers = {np.linalg.norm(g):.2e}"
          f"  (gain^L = {gain ** L:.2e})")
```

After 50 layers of width 200, the back-propagated norm is $1.8 \times 10^{-5}$ for a gain of 0.8, 1.3 for the He scale, and $1.2 \times 10^{4}$ for a gain of 1.2, in line with $g^{L}$.

The standard remedies follow from Proposition 2.8.

-   **Initialisation** at the critical scale: Glorot and Bengio (2010), He et al. (2015).
-   **Residual connections** $a_{\ell + 1} = a_\ell + g_\ell(a_\ell)$ (He et al., 2016): each Jacobian becomes $I + J_{g_\ell}$, close to the identity.
-   **Normalisation layers, gradient clipping and gated cells** (LSTM).

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 2

-   For a fixed input, a ReLU network is piecewise polynomial of degree at most $L$ in its parameters.
-   Permutation and rescaling symmetries make the objective non-convex and non-coercive.
-   Back-propagation computes the whole gradient for at most about three times the cost of a forward pass, whatever the number of parameters.
-   Gradients scale like $g^{L}$; initialisation, residual connections and normalisation keep them at scale.
:::

## 3. Landscape of the objective function {#ch3}

Whether a gradient method finds a good minimum depends on the critical points of the objective. This chapter describes them for linear networks and for wide non-linear networks.

### 3.1 Critical points and why they matter

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — Critical points]{.tag} Let $F$ be twice differentiable. A point $\theta$ with $\nabla F(\theta) = 0$ is **critical**. A local minimum that is not global is **spurious**.

A critical point that is neither a local minimum nor a local maximum is a **saddle**. Following Lee et al. (2016), a critical point is a **strict saddle** if the Hessian has a direction of negative curvature:
$$
\lambda_{\min}\big(\nabla^2 F(\theta)\big) < 0 .
$$

Such a point is never a local minimum; local maxima with a negative eigenvalue are included. $F$ has the **strict saddle property** if each of its critical points is a local minimum or a strict saddle.
:::

::: note
[What the landscape buys for optimisation]{.tag} From a random initialisation, gradient descent almost surely avoids strict saddles (Lee, Simchowitz, Jordan and Recht, 2016; Theorem 4.3). If all local minima are global, the strict saddle property holds and the iterates converge, then the limit is a global minimum for almost every initialisation.

Degenerate saddles break the argument: for the depth-3 scalar network $(abc - 1)^2$, the Hessian vanishes at the origin.
:::

### 3.2 Linear networks: no spurious minima, implicit regularisation

::: thm
[Theorem 3.2 — Baldi and Hornik (1989)]{.tag} Let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times k}$ and $B \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times d}$ with $k \le \min(m, d)$, and minimise
$$
F(A, B) = \sum_{i=1}^n \|y_i - A B x_i\|^2 .
$$

Assume that $\Sigma_{XX} = \sum_i x_i x_i^\top$ is invertible and that the matrix $\Sigma = \Sigma_{YX} \Sigma_{XX}^{-1} \Sigma_{XY}$ has full rank and distinct eigenvalues $\lambda_1 > \dots > \lambda_m$, with orthonormal eigenvectors $u_1, \dots, u_m$. Then:

-   every local minimum of $F$ is global;
-   at a global minimum, $AB = U_k U_k^\top \Sigma_{YX} \Sigma_{XX}^{-1}$, with $U_k = [u_1, \dots, u_k]$: the least-squares regressor, projected on the top-$k$ eigenvectors;
-   every other critical point with $A$ of full rank is a saddle, associated with another set of $k$ eigenvectors.

*Proof sketch.* At a critical point with $A$ of full rank, the condition in $B$ gives $AB = P_A \Sigma_{YX} \Sigma_{XX}^{-1}$, where $P_A$ is the orthogonal projector on the range of $A$.

The condition in $A$ then forces $P_A \Sigma = \Sigma P_A$. Hence the range of $A$ is spanned by $k$ eigenvectors, indexed by a set $I$.

The loss equals $\mathrm{tr}(\Sigma_{YY}) - \sum_{i \in I} \lambda_i$. If $I$ is not the top-$k$ set, rotating one eigenvector of $I$ towards a better unused one decreases the loss, so the point is a saddle. When $Y = X$, this recovers principal component analysis.
:::

::: ex
[Example 3.3 — Example 2.4 again]{.tag} For $F(a, b) = (ab - 1)^2$, the gradient is $2(ab - 1)(b, a)$. It vanishes on the hyperbola $ab = 1$ (global minima) and at the origin (a strict saddle). There is no spurious local minimum, as Theorem 3.2 predicts.
:::

Linear models also show how the algorithm selects one minimiser among many.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.4 — Implicit regularisation of gradient descent]{.tag} Let $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$ have rank $n < p$, and run gradient descent on $\tfrac12 \|Xw - y\|^2$ with a step $0 < \eta < 2/\|X\|_2^2$:
$$
w_{k + 1} = w_k - \eta\, X^\top (X w_k - y).
$$

Let $P = X^+ X$ be the orthogonal projector on the row space. Then
$$
w_k \xrightarrow[k \to \infty]{} X^+ y + (I - P)\, w_0 .
$$

From $w_0 = 0$, gradient descent converges to the minimum-norm interpolant (Proposition 0.5), although nothing in the objective asks for a small norm.

::: proof
Every update lies in $\mathrm{Im}(X^\top)$, so the component $(I - P)w_k$ never changes.

Let $w^+ = X^+ y$, which satisfies $X^\top X w^+ = X^\top y$. Then $P w_{k+1} - w^+ = (I - \eta X^\top X)(P w_k - w^+)$.

On the row space, $X^\top X$ has eigenvalues $s_i^2 \in (0, \|X\|_2^2]$, so this map is a contraction of ratio $\max_i |1 - \eta s_i^2| < 1$, and $P w_k \to w^+$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n, p = 20, 100
X, y = rng.normal(size=(n, p)), rng.normal(size=n)
step = 1 / np.linalg.norm(X, 2) ** 2
w_min_norm = np.linalg.pinv(X) @ y
P_row = np.linalg.pinv(X) @ X                           # projector on the row space of X
for name, w in [("zero init", np.zeros(p)), ("random init", rng.normal(size=p))]:
    w0 = w.copy()
    for _ in range(5000):
        w -= step * X.T @ (X @ w - y)
    print(f"{name}: residual {np.linalg.norm(X @ w - y):.1e}, "
          f"||w - w_min_norm|| = {np.linalg.norm(w - w_min_norm):.2f}, "
          f"||w - (w_min_norm + (I-P) w0)|| = {np.linalg.norm(w - w_min_norm - w0 + P_row @ w0):.1e}")
```

Both runs interpolate the data. From zero, the limit is the minimum-norm solution; from a random start, it is off by $8.93$ in norm, exactly the component $(I - P)w_0$ predicted by Proposition 3.4.

For deeper linear networks the bias is subtler, and it is governed by a conserved quantity.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.5 — Balancedness is conserved]{.tag} Let $G(A, B) = \mathcal{L}(AB)$ with $\mathcal{L}$ differentiable, and let $(A(t), B(t))$ follow the gradient flow of $G$. Then the matrix $A^\top A - B B^\top$ is constant in time.

::: proof
Write $\nabla = \nabla \mathcal{L}(AB)$. The flow is $\dot A = -\nabla B^\top$ and $\dot B = -A^\top \nabla$.

Hence the two derivatives are
$$
\frac{d}{dt}(A^\top A) = -B \nabla^\top A - A^\top \nabla B^\top, \qquad \frac{d}{dt}(B B^\top) = -A^\top \nabla B^\top - B \nabla^\top A,
$$
and they are equal. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

From a small balanced initialisation, the product follows a preconditioned flow that favours low rank (Arora, Cohen and Hazan, 2018; Gunasekar et al., 2017). Du, Hu and Lee (2018) prove the analogous conservation, unit by unit, for ReLU networks.

### 3.3 Stability of minimisers in structured linear networks

Minimisers are never isolated (Corollary 2.5), so stability must be measured modulo the symmetries: two sets of factors are close if they are close after rescaling. In the rank-one case this is a statement about directions.

:::: prop
[Proposition 3.6 — Stability of rank-one factors]{.tag} Let $u, u' \in \mathbb{R}^m$ and $v, v' \in \mathbb{R}^n$ be non-zero, $X = u v^\top$ and $X' = u' v'^\top$. Then the angle between the factors satisfies
$$
\sin \angle(u, u') \le \frac{\|X - X'\|_F}{\|X\|_F},
$$
and the same bound holds for $v$ and $v'$.

::: proof
Let $Q$ be the orthogonal projector on the orthogonal complement of $u'$, so that $Q X' = 0$.

Then, using $\|u\|\,\|v\| = \|X\|_F$,
$$
\|Q(X - X')\|_F = \|Q u\|\, \|v\| = \sin \angle(u, u')\, \|X\|_F .
$$

Since $Q$ is a contraction, $\|Q(X - X')\|_F \le \|X - X'\|_F$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The constant $1/\|X\|_F$ blows up near the origin, the saddle of Example 2.4. Malgouyres and Landsberg (official reference 7) treat products of any number of structured factors, for instance convolutional ones. Through a tensorial lifting based on the Segre embedding, they characterise when the factors are identifiable up to rescaling.

A deep analogue of the null-space property of compressed sensing then makes the error on the factors linear in the error on the product: successful training yields stable, hence interpretable, layers.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
u, v = rng.normal(size=8), rng.normal(size=6)
for scale in [1.0, 0.1]:
    Xs = scale * np.outer(u, v)
    noisy = Xs + 0.01 * rng.normal(size=Xs.shape)
    U, s, Vt = np.linalg.svd(noisy)
    X_hat = s[0] * np.outer(U[:, 0], Vt[0])            # best rank-one approximation
    sin_u = np.sqrt(max(0.0, 1 - (U[:, 0] @ u / np.linalg.norm(u)) ** 2))
    bound = np.linalg.norm(X_hat - Xs) / np.linalg.norm(Xs)
    print(f"||X||_F = {np.linalg.norm(Xs):5.2f}: sin(angle(u_hat, u)) = {sin_u:.4f} <= bound {bound:.4f}")
```

With the same noise, the factor direction is recovered to $\sin\angle = 0.017$ when $\|X\|_F = 2.15$, but only to 0.125 when $\|X\|_F = 0.21$, each time below the bound of Proposition 3.6.

### 3.4 Non-linear networks: the benefit of width

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.7 — A wide last hidden layer has no bad critical points]{.tag} Write $f_\theta(x) = V^\top \phi_\psi(x)$, where $\phi_\psi(x) \in \mathbb{R}^m$ gathers the last hidden layer (parameters $\psi$) and $V \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times c}$ the output weights. Let $\Phi_\psi \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times m}$ stack the features of the $N$ training points, and
$$
F(\psi, V) = \tfrac12 \|\Phi_\psi V - Y\|_F^2 .
$$

If $(\psi, V)$ is critical and $\Phi_\psi$ has rank $N$ (which requires $m \ge N$), then $F(\psi, V) = 0$: the point is a global minimum.

::: proof
The gradient in $V$ is $\Phi_\psi^\top (\Phi_\psi V - Y)$, and it vanishes at a critical point.

Since $\Phi_\psi$ has rank $N$, the map $r \mapsto \Phi_\psi^\top r$ is injective on $\mathbb{R}^N$, so the residual $\Phi_\psi V - Y$ is zero. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Bad critical points can therefore only occur where the features lose rank. Nguyen and Hein turn this mechanism into a statement about almost all parameters.

::: thm
[Theorem 3.8 — Nguyen and Hein (2017), statement]{.tag} Consider a fully connected network with the square loss and an analytic activation, such as the sigmoid or the softplus. Suppose one hidden layer has more units than there are training points, and the widths do not increase from that layer to the output (a pyramidal structure).

Then, under mild conditions on the data and the activation, almost all local minima are global. The proof shows that the feature matrix of the wide layer has rank $N$ for almost every choice of the lower weights, and extends the argument of Theorem 3.7 through the upper layers.
:::

Venturi, Bandeira and Bruna (official reference 5) show that wide enough networks of finite intrinsic dimension have no spurious valleys; Safran and Shamir (official reference 6) that over-specified networks often start in a good basin. Width is not sufficient in general: Safran and Shamir (2018) exhibit spurious local minima in two-layer ReLU networks of moderate width.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 3

-   Two-layer linear networks have no spurious local minima; their other critical points are saddles.
-   From zero, gradient descent on under-determined least squares converges to the minimum-norm interpolant.
-   Factors of a product are stable only modulo rescaling, and not near the zero product.
-   A hidden layer wider than the data set removes bad critical points where its features have full rank.
:::

## 4. Non-convex optimisation {#ch4}

Chapter 3 described the landscape. This chapter follows the iterates of gradient methods through it: which critical points they avoid, whether they converge, and how fast.

### 4.1 Gradient descent on smooth functions

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.1 — Stationarity at rate 1/√K]{.tag} Let $F$ have an $L$-Lipschitz gradient and be bounded below by $F^\ast$. Gradient descent with step $1/L$ satisfies
$$
\min_{k < K} \|\nabla F(x_k)\|^2 \le \frac{2L\, (F(x_0) - F^\ast)}{K} .
$$

::: proof
By the descent lemma (Proposition 0.2), each step decreases $F$ by at least $\|\nabla F(x_k)\|^2/(2L)$. Summing over $k < K$, the total decrease, at most $F(x_0) - F^\ast$, bounds $K/(2L)$ times the minimum. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The theorem says nothing about *which* critical point is approached, nor whether the iterates converge at all. The next two sections answer these questions.

### 4.2 Morse functions and strict saddles

::: def
[Definition 4.2 — Morse function]{.tag} A twice differentiable function is **Morse** if the Hessian is invertible at every critical point. Its critical points are then isolated, and each one is a local minimum, a local maximum or a strict saddle.
:::

Training objectives are never Morse, since their minimisers come in continuous families (Corollary 2.5). Lee and coauthors treat one strict saddle at a time. Panageas and Piliouras (official reference 2) cover non-isolated critical points, which gives the first statement below.

::: thm
[Theorem 4.3 — Gradient descent only converges to minimisers (Lee, Simchowitz, Jordan and Recht, 2016; Panageas and Piliouras, 2017)]{.tag} Let $F$ be twice continuously differentiable with an $L$-Lipschitz gradient, and run gradient descent with a step $0 < \eta < 1/L$. The set of initial points from which the iterates converge to a strict saddle has Lebesgue measure zero.

For a Morse function, if the iterates converge, then for almost every initialisation the limit is a local minimum.

*Proof sketch.*

1.  The map $g(x) = x - \eta \nabla F(x)$ is a diffeomorphism: its Jacobian $I - \eta \nabla^2 F$ is invertible because $\eta \|\nabla^2 F\| < 1$.
2.  At a strict saddle $x^\ast$, the Jacobian of $g$ has an eigenvalue $1 - \eta \lambda_{\min} > 1$. The centre-stable manifold theorem puts all points whose orbit stays near $x^\ast$ on a manifold of dimension less than $p$, a null set.
3.  The points that converge to $x^\ast$ are preimages of this null set under the iterates of $g$. The inverse of $g$ is $C^1$ and maps null sets to null sets, so this countable union is null.
4.  Cover the strict saddles by countably many such neighbourhoods (Lindelöf's lemma) to conclude.
:::

::: ex
[Example 4.4 — Avoiding a saddle]{.tag} Let $F(x, y) = x^4/4 - x^2/2 + y^2/2$. Its critical points are the minima $(\pm 1, 0)$ and the strict saddle $(0, 0)$, with Hessian $\mathrm{diag}(-1, 1)$. The iterates converge to the saddle only from its stable manifold, the line $x = 0$.
:::

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
grad = lambda z: np.stack([z[:, 0] ** 3 - z[:, 0], z[:, 1]], axis=1)
Z = rng.uniform(-2, 2, size=(10_000, 2))           # 10 000 random initialisations
for _ in range(500):
    Z = Z - 0.1 * grad(Z)
print("limits reached:", np.unique(np.round(Z, 6) + 0.0, axis=0).tolist())
z = np.array([[0.0, 1.5]])                          # start on the stable manifold {x = 0}
for _ in range(500):
    z = z - 0.1 * grad(z)
print("start (0, 1.5) ->", np.round(z, 6).tolist())
```

All 10 000 random starts end at $(-1, 0)$ or $(1, 0)$; the start $(0, 1.5)$, on the stable manifold, ends at the saddle.

### 4.3 The Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz property

Bounded gradient iterates may still fail to converge: on some smooth functions they circle forever around a ring of minimisers (Absil, Mahony and Andrews, 2005). The Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz property rules this out.

::: def
[Definition 4.5 — Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz (KL) property]{.tag} A differentiable $F$ has the KL property at $\bar x$ if there are $\eta > 0$, a neighbourhood $U$ of $\bar x$ and a *desingularising function* $\varphi$, such that the inequality below holds.

Here $\varphi : [0, \eta) \to [0, \infty)$ is concave and continuous, $\varphi(0) = 0$, and $\varphi$ is $C^1$ and increasing on $(0, \eta)$. The inequality is
$$
\varphi'\big(F(x) - F(\bar x)\big)\, \|\nabla F(x)\| \ge 1
$$
for every $x \in U$ with $F(\bar x) < F(x) < F(\bar x) + \eta$.

With $\varphi(s) = c\, s^{1 - \vartheta}$ this is the Łojasiewicz inequality, with exponent $\vartheta \in [0, 1)$:
$$
|F(x) - F(\bar x)|^{\vartheta} \le C\, \|\nabla F(x)\| .
$$
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 4.6 — Algebraic and geometric properties of deep learning losses]{.tag}

-   Real-analytic functions satisfy the Łojasiewicz inequality (Łojasiewicz, 1963).
-   Functions definable in an o-minimal structure satisfy the KL property at every point: Kurdyka (1998) in the smooth case, Bolte, Daniilidis, Lewis and Shiota (2007) for non-smooth functions and Clarke subgradients.
-   Semi-algebraic functions are definable. By Proposition 2.1, the empirical risk of a ReLU network with the square, absolute or hinge loss is semi-algebraic.
-   With sigmoids, softmax and cross-entropy, the objective is definable in the structure generated by the exponential, which is o-minimal (Wilkie, 1996).

The usual training objectives therefore have the KL property everywhere. The proofs belong to o-minimal (tame) geometry (van den Dries, 1998).
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.7 — Convergence of gradient descent under KL]{.tag} Let $F$ have an $L$-Lipschitz gradient and the KL property at every point, and run gradient descent with step $\eta \le 1/L$. If the iterates are bounded, they have finite length and converge to a critical point:
$$
\sum_{k} \|x_{k+1} - x_k\| < \infty .
$$

::: proof
Let $\Delta_k = x_{k+1} - x_k = -\eta \nabla F(x_k)$, let $\bar x$ be a cluster point, and let $r_k = F(x_k) - F(\bar x)$, which decreases to $0$.

*Sufficient decrease.* The descent lemma with $\eta \le 1/L$ gives $r_k - r_{k+1} \ge \|\Delta_k\|^2 / (2\eta)$.

*KL step.* For $k$ large, $x_k \in U$, and the KL inequality reads $\varphi'(r_k) \ge \eta / \|\Delta_k\|$. By concavity,
$$
\varphi(r_k) - \varphi(r_{k+1}) \ge \varphi'(r_k)\,(r_k - r_{k+1}) \ge \tfrac12 \|\Delta_k\| .
$$

*Conclusion.* Summing telescopes into $\sum_k \|\Delta_k\| \le 2\varphi(r_{k_0})$. Finite length makes $(x_k)$ a Cauchy sequence; its limit is critical because $\nabla F(x_k) = -\Delta_k/\eta \to 0$.

That the iterates stay in $U$ after some $k_0$ follows from the same estimate by induction (Attouch and Bolte, 2009). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The exponent gives the rate: $\vartheta = 1/2$ yields linear convergence, and $\vartheta \in (1/2, 1)$ a polynomial rate. Bolte, Sabach and Teboulle (official reference 1) isolate the three ingredients of this proof — sufficient decrease, a relative error bound, KL — and apply them to proximal alternating minimisation over blocks of variables, such as the layers of a network or the factors of a matrix factorisation.

### 4.4 Global convergence: least squares under surjectivity, stochastic gradient

When the Jacobian of the outputs stays surjective along training, which requires over-parameterisation, the KL inequality holds globally with exponent $1/2$, and gradient descent reaches a global minimum.

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.8 — Least squares under a surjectivity assumption]{.tag} Let $G : \mathbb{R}^p \to \mathbb{R}^N$ map the parameters to the outputs on the $N$ training points, $J(\theta)$ its Jacobian and $F(\theta) = \tfrac12 \|G(\theta) - y\|^2$. Assume that, on a set containing the iterates, $\nabla F$ is $\beta$-Lipschitz and
$$
\lambda_{\min}\big(J(\theta) J(\theta)^\top\big) \ge \mu > 0 .
$$

Then gradient descent with step $\eta \le 1/\beta$ satisfies

::: key
[Key result — linear convergence under the PL inequality]{.tag}
$$
F(\theta_k) \le (1 - \eta \mu)^k\, F(\theta_0) .
$$
:::

::: proof
With $r = G(\theta) - y$, the gradient is $J^\top r$. Hence $\|\nabla F\|^2 = r^\top J J^\top r \ge \mu \|r\|^2 = 2\mu F$: this is the Polyak–Łojasiewicz inequality.

The descent lemma then gives
$$
F(\theta_{k+1}) \le F(\theta_k) - \tfrac{\eta}{2}\|\nabla F(\theta_k)\|^2 \le (1 - \eta\mu)\, F(\theta_k).
$$

[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Surjectivity of $J$ needs at least as many parameters as data points ($p \ge N$). For a wide two-layer network, $\mu$ is bounded below at initialisation and the Jacobian barely moves during training, the lazy regime of [ch. 11](#ch11).

```python
import torch

torch.set_num_threads(1)                            # tiny model: one thread is fastest
torch.manual_seed(0)
N, d, m = 20, 20, 2000
X = torch.randn(N, d); X = X / X.norm(dim=1, keepdim=True)
y = torch.randn(N)

def outputs(theta):                                 # f(x) = a^T relu(W x) / sqrt(m)
    W, a = theta[: m * d].view(m, d), theta[m * d:]
    return torch.relu(X @ W.T) @ a / m ** 0.5

def spectrum(theta):                                # extreme eigenvalues of J J^T
    J = torch.autograd.functional.jacobian(outputs, theta.detach())
    e = torch.linalg.eigvalsh(J @ J.T)
    return e[0].item(), e[-1].item()

theta = torch.randn(m * d + m, requires_grad=True)
mu, lam = spectrum(theta)
lr = 0.2                                            # below 1 / lambda_max
opt, losses = torch.optim.SGD([theta], lr=lr), []
for t in range(201):
    loss = 0.5 * ((outputs(theta) - y) ** 2).sum()
    losses.append(loss.item())
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
print(f"at init: mu = {mu:.3f}, lambda_max = {lam:.2f}; after training: mu = {spectrum(theta)[0]:.3f}")
print("loss at steps 0, 50, 100, 200:", [f"{losses[k]:.1e}" for k in (0, 50, 100, 200)])
print(f"guaranteed rate 1 - lr*mu = {1 - lr * mu:.3f}; "
      f"observed rate per step = {(losses[200] / losses[100]) ** 0.01:.3f}")
```

With 2 000 hidden units and 20 data points, $\mu = 0.274$ at initialisation and $0.271$ after training. The loss falls from $15$ to $3.9 \times 10^{-10}$ in 200 steps, at an observed rate of $0.900$ per step, faster than the guaranteed $0.945$.

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.9 — Stochastic gradient on a smooth non-convex function (Ghadimi and Lan, 2013)]{.tag} Let $F$ have an $L$-Lipschitz gradient and be bounded below by $F^\ast$, and run $x_{k+1} = x_k - \eta g_k$.

Here $g_k$ is an unbiased estimate of $\nabla F(x_k)$, with variance at most $\sigma^2$. If $\eta \le 1/L$, then
$$
\frac1K \sum_{k < K} \mathbb{E}\|\nabla F(x_k)\|^2 \le \frac{2\,(F(x_0) - F^\ast)}{\eta K} + L \eta \sigma^2 .
$$

The choice $\eta \propto 1/\sqrt{K}$ gives the rate $O(1/\sqrt{K})$.

::: proof
The second moment of $g_k$ is $\|\nabla F(x_k)\|^2$ plus the variance. The descent lemma in conditional expectation then gives
$$
\mathbb{E} F(x_{k+1}) \le \mathbb{E} F(x_k) - \frac{\eta}{2}\, \mathbb{E}\|\nabla F(x_k)\|^2 + \frac{L\eta^2\sigma^2}{2} .
$$

Sum over $k < K$ and divide by $\eta K/2$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

ReLU networks are not smooth, but they are definable. For such locally Lipschitz functions, Davis, Drusvyatskiy, Kakade and Lee (official reference 24) prove that the stochastic subgradient method with decreasing steps has, almost surely, only Clarke-critical limit points, under a boundedness assumption.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 4

-   Gradient descent finds an $\varepsilon$-stationary point in $O(1/\varepsilon^2)$ steps and almost surely avoids strict saddles.
-   Deep learning objectives are definable, hence KL: bounded iterates converge.
-   A surjective Jacobian gives the PL inequality and linear convergence to a global minimum.
-   Stochastic gradient reaches stationarity at rate $O(1/\sqrt{K})$.
:::

## 5. Robust deep learning I: stability, interpretability, Bayesian uncertainty {#ch5}

A network deployed in a hospital or a car must be accurate, but also predictable. A small change of the input should not flip the decision, and the network should signal when it does not know. This chapter introduces both sides of decision robustness: stability and uncertainty.

### 5.1 Decision robustness for critical systems

In medical diagnosis or autonomous driving, errors have asymmetric and sometimes irreversible costs. A deployed model must then answer three questions besides “what is the prediction?”.

-   Is the decision stable under small perturbations of the input (5.1–5.2)?
-   Which training data does it rest on (5.3)?
-   How uncertain is it, and is the input of the kind seen in training (5.4, [ch. 6](#ch6), [ch. 7](#ch7))?

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — Lipschitz stability and certified margin]{.tag} A map $f$ is $L$-Lipschitz if $\|f(x) - f(x')\| \le L \|x - x'\|$ for all inputs. For a classifier with logits $f$ and predicted class $y$, the **margin** is $m(x) = f_y(x) - \max_{k \ne y} f_k(x)$.

If $f$ is $L$-Lipschitz in the Euclidean norm, each difference $f_y - f_k$ is $\sqrt2 L$-Lipschitz. The decision is therefore unchanged on the ball
$$
\|\delta\| < \frac{m(x)}{\sqrt2\, L} .
$$
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 5.2 — A Lipschitz bound for networks]{.tag} If every activation is 1-Lipschitz (ReLU and tanh are; the sigmoid is even 1/4-Lipschitz), then
$$
\mathrm{Lip}(f_\theta) \le \prod_{\ell = 1}^L \|W_\ell\|_2 .
$$

*Proof*: each layer $a \mapsto \sigma(W_\ell a + b_\ell)$ is $\|W_\ell\|_2$-Lipschitz; compose, as in Proposition 2.8. The bound is often very pessimistic, but it is what spectral normalisation controls.
:::

::: ex
[Example 5.3 — Why high dimension makes linear models fragile]{.tag} For a linear score $w^\top x$, the perturbation $\delta = \varepsilon\, \mathrm{sign}(w)$, of max-norm $\varepsilon$, changes the score by $\varepsilon \|w\|_1$.

Take 3072 inputs (a 32 × 32 colour image), weights of size 0.1 and $\varepsilon = 1/255$, an invisible change. The score moves by
$$
\varepsilon \|w\|_1 = 3072 \times 0.1 / 255 \approx 1.2 .
$$

The effect grows linearly with the dimension. This is the explanation of adversarial examples given by Goodfellow, Shlens and Szegedy (2015), whose attack takes $\delta = \varepsilon\, \mathrm{sign}(\nabla_x \ell)$.
:::

### 5.2 Stability to deformations

Images of the same object differ by small deformations more than by additive noise.

::: def
[Definition 5.4 — Stability to deformations]{.tag} Let $\tau : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d$ be a smooth displacement field and $(L_\tau x)(u) = x(u - \tau(u))$ the deformed signal. A representation $\Phi$ is **stable to deformations** if, for some constant $C$,
$$
\|\Phi(L_\tau x) - \Phi(x)\| \le C\, \|x\|\, \big(\|\nabla \tau\|_\infty + \text{higher-order terms in } \tau\big).
$$

Invariance to translations alone is not enough: the modulus of the Fourier transform is translation-invariant, but a small dilation moves its high frequencies far away.
:::

-   **Scattering networks** (Bruna and Mallat, 2013; the theory is in Mallat, 2012) cascade wavelet transforms and complex moduli, then average at a scale $2^J$. They are invariant to translations small compared with $2^J$ and Lipschitz-stable to deformations, with a bound that vanishes with the amplitude of $\tau$ relative to $2^J$ and with the sizes of $\nabla\tau$ and of the Hessian of $\tau$.
-   **Convolutional kernel representations** (Bietti and Mairal, 2017) satisfy similar bounds. Pooling and patch sizes trade invariance against discriminative power, and the stability of a learned model is controlled by its norm in the associated reproducing kernel Hilbert space.

### 5.3 Influence functions: which training points drive a prediction?

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.5 — Influence of a training point (Koh and Liang, 2017)]{.tag} Let $\hat\theta$ minimise $\widehat R(\theta) = \frac1n \sum_i \ell(z_i, \theta)$, twice differentiable with invertible Hessian $H$ at $\hat\theta$.

Up-weight a point $z$ by $\varepsilon$, and let $\hat\theta_\varepsilon$ minimise $\widehat R(\theta) + \varepsilon\, \ell(z, \theta)$. Then
$$
\frac{d \hat\theta_\varepsilon}{d\varepsilon}\Big|_{\varepsilon = 0} = -H^{-1} \nabla_\theta \ell(z, \hat\theta).
$$

For a test point, the loss changes at the rate
$$
\frac{d}{d\varepsilon}\, \ell(z_{\mathrm{test}}, \hat\theta_\varepsilon)\Big|_{\varepsilon = 0} = -\nabla_\theta \ell(z_{\mathrm{test}}, \hat\theta)^\top H^{-1} \nabla_\theta \ell(z, \hat\theta).
$$

Removing $z$ from the training set corresponds to $\varepsilon = -1/n$.

::: proof
The optimality condition defines $\hat\theta_\varepsilon$ implicitly:
$$
\nabla \widehat R(\hat\theta_\varepsilon) + \varepsilon\, \nabla \ell(z, \hat\theta_\varepsilon) = 0 .
$$

The implicit function theorem applies since $H$ is invertible. Differentiating at $\varepsilon = 0$ gives $H\, \dot\theta + \nabla \ell(z, \hat\theta) = 0$, where $\dot\theta$ is the derivative of $\hat\theta_\varepsilon$. The test-loss formula is the chain rule. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

This classical tool of robust statistics (Cook and Weisberg, 1982) explains a prediction by the training points that support it. It also finds mislabelled examples and crafts training-set attacks. For networks, $H$ is not invertible, and Koh and Liang use a damping term and Hessian-vector products.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, d, lam = 200, 5, 1e-2
X = rng.normal(size=(n, d)); w_true = rng.normal(size=d)
y = (rng.uniform(size=n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-X @ w_true))).astype(float)
x_test, y_test = rng.normal(size=d), 1.0

def fit(X, y, iters=30):                     # Newton's method on the L2-regularised log-loss
    w = np.zeros(d)
    for _ in range(iters):
        p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-X @ w))
        g = X.T @ (p - y) / len(y) + lam * w
        H = (X.T * (p * (1 - p))) @ X / len(y) + lam * np.eye(d)
        w -= np.linalg.solve(H, g)
    return w, H

def test_loss(w):
    p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-x_test @ w))
    return -np.log(p if y_test == 1 else 1 - p)

w_hat, H = fit(X, y)
p_t = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-x_test @ w_hat))
g_test = (p_t - y_test) * x_test
predicted, actual = [], []
for i in range(n):
    p_i = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-X[i] @ w_hat))
    g_i = (p_i - y[i]) * X[i] + lam * w_hat          # gradient of the i-th summand
    predicted.append(g_test @ np.linalg.solve(H, g_i) / n)   # removing z_i: eps = -1/n
    w_loo, _ = fit(np.delete(X, i, 0), np.delete(y, i))
    actual.append(test_loss(w_loo) - test_loss(w_hat))
predicted, actual = np.array(predicted), np.array(actual)
print(f"correlation(influence prediction, leave-one-out) = {np.corrcoef(predicted, actual)[0, 1]:.4f}")
top = np.argsort(-np.abs(actual))[:3]
print("three most influential points (predicted, actual):",
      [(int(i), round(float(predicted[i]), 4), round(float(actual[i]), 4)) for i in top])
```

On this L2-regularised logistic regression, the influence formula and 200 refits by leave-one-out agree with correlation $0.9998$. For the most influential point, it predicts a test-loss change of $0.161$, against $0.169$ measured.

### 5.4 Decision uncertainty and Bayesian models

::: def
[Definition 5.6 — Typology of uncertainty]{.tag}

-   **Aleatoric** uncertainty is the randomness of $Y$ given $X$: overlapping classes, sensor noise. It does not decrease with more data.
-   **Epistemic** uncertainty is the lack of knowledge of the model: it is large far from the training data and decreases as data accumulate.
-   **Distribution shift** occurs when test inputs come from another distribution than the training inputs; it is treated in [ch. 7](#ch7).
:::

::: def
[Definition 5.7 — Bayesian model, posterior and predictive distribution]{.tag} A prior $p(\theta)$ and a likelihood, the product of the terms $p(y_i \mid x_i, \theta)$, define the posterior and the predictive distribution:
$$
p(\theta \mid \mathcal{D}) \propto p(\mathcal{D} \mid \theta)\, p(\theta), \qquad p(y \mid x, \mathcal{D}) = \int p(y \mid x, \theta)\, p(\theta \mid \mathcal{D})\, d\theta .
$$

The spread of the posterior, pushed through the predictions, is the epistemic uncertainty.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.8 — Bayesian linear regression]{.tag} Let $y = w^\top \phi(x) + \varepsilon$ with noise $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \beta^{-1})$, an explicit embedding $\phi(x) \in \mathbb{R}^D$, and the prior $w \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \alpha^{-1} I)$. With $\Phi$ the design matrix, the posterior is $\mathcal{N}(m_N, S_N)$ with
$$
S_N^{-1} = \alpha I + \beta\, \Phi^\top \Phi, \qquad m_N = \beta\, S_N \Phi^\top y .
$$

The predictive distribution at $x$ is Gaussian, with mean $m_N^\top \phi(x)$ and variance

::: key
[Key result — the predictive variance splits in two]{.tag}
$$
\sigma_N^2(x) = \underbrace{\beta^{-1}}_{\text{aleatoric}} + \underbrace{\phi(x)^\top S_N\, \phi(x)}_{\text{epistemic}} .
$$
:::

::: proof
The posterior is Proposition 0.4 with $m_0 = 0$ and $S_0 = \alpha^{-1} I$. Under the posterior, $y = w^\top \phi(x) + \varepsilon$ is a sum of two independent Gaussian variables; means and variances add. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The model is linear in $w$ but not in $x$: with polynomial features, Gaussian bumps or random features, it performs non-linear regression. The first lab fits it on simulated data with a gap.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = np.concatenate([rng.uniform(-2, 0, 30), rng.uniform(1, 2, 15)])   # gap on (0, 1)
beta = 25.0                                          # noise precision (sigma = 0.2)
y = np.sin(2 * x) + rng.normal(0, beta ** -0.5, x.size)

centres = np.linspace(-3, 3, 25)                     # explicit embedding: Gaussian bumps
phi = lambda t: np.exp(-(np.subtract.outer(t, centres) ** 2) / (2 * 0.4 ** 2))

alpha = 1.0                                          # prior w ~ N(0, alpha^{-1} I)
Phi = phi(x)
S_N = np.linalg.inv(alpha * np.eye(centres.size) + beta * Phi.T @ Phi)
m_N = beta * S_N @ Phi.T @ y

for t in [-1.0, 0.5, 1.5, 3.0]:
    f = phi(np.array([t]))[0]
    mean, var = f @ m_N, 1 / beta + f @ S_N @ f      # predictive mean and variance
    print(f"x = {t:4.1f}: mean {mean:+.2f} (truth {np.sin(2 * t):+.2f}), "
          f"predictive std {np.sqrt(var):.2f} (noise std {beta ** -0.5:.2f})")
```

Where data are dense ($x = -1$ and $x = 1.5$), the predictive standard deviation is 0.22 and 0.21, barely above the noise level 0.20. It rises to 0.59 in the gap and to 1.31 outside the data, at $x = 3$: the epistemic term does its job.

::: recap
Key takeaways — chapter 5

-   A Lipschitz constant and a margin certify a decision on a ball.
-   Scattering and convolutional kernel representations are stable to small deformations.
-   Influence functions predict, through one Hessian solve, the effect of a training point.
-   Bayesian linear regression adds an epistemic term that grows away from the data.
:::

## 6. Robust deep learning II: Bayesian neural networks {#ch6}

For a network, the posterior is neither Gaussian nor computable. This chapter presents the three approximations used in practice — Laplace, variational and Monte Carlo dropout — first on logistic regression, where they can be checked.

### 6.1 The Laplace approximation

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — Laplace approximation]{.tag} Let $\theta_{\mathrm{MAP}}$ maximise the log-posterior and $H$ be the Hessian of the negative log-posterior there. The Laplace approximation is the Gaussian
$$
q(\theta) = \mathcal{N}\big(\theta_{\mathrm{MAP}}, H^{-1}\big),
$$
obtained from the second-order Taylor expansion of the log-posterior at its maximum.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 6.2 — Logistic regression]{.tag} Let $p(y = 1 \mid x, w) = s(w^\top \phi(x))$ with the logistic function $s$, and the prior $\mathcal{N}(0, \alpha^{-1} I)$. With $s_i = s(w^\top \phi_i)$, the Hessian of the negative log-posterior is
$$
H(w) = \alpha I + \sum_i s_i (1 - s_i)\, \phi_i \phi_i^\top .
$$

It is positive definite, so the MAP is unique and Newton's method finds it. *Proof*: the gradient is $\alpha w + \sum_i (s_i - y_i)\phi_i$, and $s' = s(1 - s)$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.3 — Predictive probability: the probit approximation (MacKay, 1992)]{.tag} Under $q$, the activation $a = w^\top \phi(x)$ is Gaussian, with mean $\mu_a = \theta_{\mathrm{MAP}}^\top \phi(x)$ and variance $s_a^2 = \phi(x)^\top H^{-1} \phi(x)$. Then
$$
p(y = 1 \mid x, \mathcal{D}) \approx s\big(\kappa(s_a^2)\, \mu_a\big), \qquad \kappa(s^2) = \big(1 + \pi s^2/8\big)^{-1/2} .
$$

::: proof
Replace $s(a)$ by the probit $\Phi(\lambda a)$, where $\Phi$ is the standard Gaussian distribution function and $\lambda^2 = \pi/8$, which has the same slope at 0. A Gaussian average of a probit is a probit:
$$
\int \Phi(\lambda a)\, \mathcal{N}(a; \mu, s^2)\, da = \Phi\big(\lambda \mu / \sqrt{1 + \lambda^2 s^2}\big).
$$

Converting back to the logistic function gives the formula. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

The approximation pulls the probability towards $1/2$ where $s_a^2$ is large, without changing the predicted class.

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 100                                               # two Gaussian classes in the plane
X = np.vstack([rng.normal([-1, 0], 0.7, (n, 2)), rng.normal([1, 0], 0.7, (n, 2))])
y = np.r_[np.zeros(n), np.ones(n)]
Phi = np.c_[np.ones(2 * n), X]                        # features (1, x1, x2)
alpha = 1.0                                           # prior w ~ N(0, alpha^{-1} I)
sigmoid = lambda a: 1 / (1 + np.exp(-a))

w = np.zeros(3)                                       # MAP by Newton's method
for _ in range(25):
    p = sigmoid(Phi @ w)
    H = (Phi.T * (p * (1 - p))) @ Phi + alpha * np.eye(3)
    w -= np.linalg.solve(H, Phi.T @ (p - y) + alpha * w)
S = np.linalg.inv(H)                                  # Laplace: q(w) = N(w_MAP, H^{-1})

for x in [np.array([0.5, 0.0]), np.array([0.5, 8.0]), np.array([6.0, 8.0])]:
    f = np.r_[1.0, x]
    mu_a, s2_a = f @ w, f @ S @ f
    probit = sigmoid(mu_a / np.sqrt(1 + np.pi * s2_a / 8))
    mc = sigmoid(rng.multivariate_normal(w, S, 20_000) @ f).mean()
    print(f"x = ({x[0]:.1f}, {x[1]:.1f}): MAP {sigmoid(mu_a):.3f} | Laplace, probit {probit:.3f} | "
          f"Laplace, Monte Carlo {mc:.3f} | var(a) = {s2_a:.2f}")
```

Near the data, at the point (0.5, 0), the MAP gives 0.869 and the Laplace predictive 0.864. Far along the uninformative direction, at (0.5, 8), the activation variance is 6.8, and the Laplace predictive moves from 0.345 to 0.417, towards 1/2. The probit formula and a Monte Carlo average over $q$ agree within 0.004.

For networks, Laplace is applied to the last layer or with Kronecker-factored Hessians (Ritter, Botev and Barber, 2018; Daxberger et al., 2021).

### 6.2 Variational inference and Bayes by Backprop

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.4 — Evidence lower bound]{.tag} For every density $q$ on the parameters,
$$
\log p(\mathcal{D}) = \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q}\big[\log p(\mathcal{D} \mid \theta)\big] - \mathrm{KL}\big(q \,\|\, p(\theta)\big)}_{\mathrm{ELBO}(q)} + \mathrm{KL}\big(q \,\|\, p(\theta \mid \mathcal{D})\big).
$$

Maximising the ELBO over a family of distributions is therefore minimising the KL divergence to the posterior.

::: proof
For every $\theta$, Bayes' rule gives
$$
\log p(\mathcal{D}) = \log p(\mathcal{D} \mid \theta) + \log p(\theta) - \log p(\theta \mid \mathcal{D}).
$$

Take the expectation under $q$, then add and subtract $\mathbb{E}_q[\log q(\theta)]$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 6.5 — Bayes by Backprop (Blundell et al., 2015)]{.tag} Take a mean-field Gaussian family, $q(\theta) = \prod_j \mathcal{N}(\mu_j, \sigma_j^2)$ with $\sigma_j = \log(1 + e^{\rho_j})$, and write $\theta = \mu + \sigma \odot \varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)$.

This **reparameterisation** (Kingma and Welling, 2014) turns the expectation of the ELBO into an expectation over $\varepsilon$, which no longer depends on $(\mu, \rho)$. One draw of $\varepsilon$ then gives an unbiased gradient by back-propagation.

With a standard normal prior, the KL term is explicit:
$$
\mathrm{KL}(q \,\|\, p) = \sum_j \Big(\frac{\sigma_j^2 + \mu_j^2 - 1}{2} - \log \sigma_j\Big).
$$
:::

### 6.3 Dropout: a regulariser and a variational approximation

Dropout (Srivastava et al., 2014) multiplies each unit by an independent Bernoulli mask $\delta \sim \mathcal{B}(q)$, divided by the keep probability $q$, during training. On a linear model, its effect is an explicit penalty.

:::: prop
[Proposition 6.6 — Dropout is a data-dependent ridge]{.tag} In linear regression, replace each input $x_{ij}$ by $x_{ij} \delta_{ij}/q$ with independent $\delta_{ij} \sim \mathcal{B}(q)$. The expected training loss is
$$
\mathbb{E}_\delta \sum_i \big(y_i - \tilde x_i^\top w\big)^2 = \sum_i \big(y_i - x_i^\top w\big)^2 + \frac{1 - q}{q} \sum_j w_j^2 \sum_i x_{ij}^2 .
$$

::: proof
For each $i$, the random variable $\tilde x_i^\top w$ has mean $x_i^\top w$ and variance $\sum_j x_{ij}^2 w_j^2 (1 - q)/q$, since $\mathrm{Var}(\delta/q) = (1 - q)/q$. Conclude with the bias–variance identity
$$
\mathbb{E}(y - Z)^2 = (y - \mathbb{E}Z)^2 + \mathrm{Var}\, Z .
$$

[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

Dropout is thus a ridge penalty weighted by the energy of each feature; Wager, Wang and Liang (2013) extend this reading to generalised linear models. Its Bayesian reading is due to Gal and Ghahramani.

::: thm
[Theorem 6.7 — Monte Carlo dropout (Gal and Ghahramani, 2016), statement]{.tag} Consider a network with dropout before every weight layer, trained with weight decay. Its training objective coincides, up to constants and an approximation of the KL term, with the negative ELBO of a variational family in which each weight matrix is $M\, \mathrm{diag}(\delta)$, with Bernoulli $\delta$ and learned $M$, against a Gaussian prior.

Keeping dropout active at test time and averaging $T$ stochastic passes therefore estimates the predictive mean, and the spread of the passes estimates the epistemic variance. The key step approximates the KL divergence between the variational distribution and the prior by a weight-decay penalty on $M$.
:::

The second lab implements a `LinearVariational` layer and compares it with MC dropout on a one-dimensional regression with a gap.

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
```
